And by the way, that is working remarkably well. We've reduced our jail backlog by over 90%. We've saved the state of Georgia about $24 million a year. on just that part of it. In the first quarter of this year, we had about 4,100 people who are in accountability courts. That's drug courts, DUI courts, mental health courts, veterans courts, trying to deal with the problems that individuals face coming from various backgrounds, including, as I said, the veteran community. Now, almost all 4100 of those would have been in our expensive $18,000 bid prison system but for the front end adjustments. We've been recognized by the way as having the best drug court system in the entire country. The second leg was a juvenile justice reform following a similar model, diverting those non-violent juveniles out of our RYDCs and YDCs, and we're seeing the same kind of remarkable savings in dollars but also changing directions of people's lives. The third leg was dealing with the most difficult part, and that is the 55 to 60,000 people. who make up our prison population. Almost all of whom at some point in time are going to be released. Either they will have served their entire Senate or they will be parole. Now we did a survey to determine why is it that only that one out of every three that's released is back in our system within three years or less. The major conclusion we reached was They don't have a high school diploma or GED. 70% of them do not. So we're working on that aspect. We've hired one of the better local school superintendents, and I think you probably know him. He was the superintendent of the Versailles County School System, one of the best school systems in our state. And Buster Evans is doing a great job as an assistant commissioner of our Department of Corrections. And we're going to change that dynamic. But even when we change that dynamic, when somebody has a major felony on their record and they are released, we want them to have a marketable job skill. But even with that, they have great difficulty because most of them have lost contact with their families. They've either been disowned or just lost altogether any support group in the civilian society. churches can fill that void and that's why we've reached out to the faith-based community and we've had a great response because the pattern is if someone's released from our prison they go back to the same community where they got in trouble in the first place and if the local community including the faith-based community, does not provide some assistance for them, then the likelihood of them getting in more trouble is greatly increased. We want to have churches across our state who are going to say, we're willing to be a part of the solution. We recognize the importance of that. We want individuals who are in that situation to have a safe haven that they can come to, to ask us for counseling, to ask us to help them find a place to live, to ask us for helping them get a job. That's what churches do now. But if this third leg of criminal justice reform is to be totally successful, we have to have their help in making it work.
